mappings.note: Statement set mixing what the Rig Veda and Vishnu Purana say (LO-86) with whether Tianzhu is Chinese or Greek (LO-98). Both registers must be known to answer.

Which of Jambudvipa and Hindustan is attested earlier: the first is an indigenous textual name (LO-86), the second a Persian coinage (LO-98), and the item turns on dating the two traditions against each other.
Sifts four claims and keeps 'Xuanzang was a Chinese visitor' - the correct option is entirely about a foreign contact, so LO-98.
Decodes 'Hidu' in a 6th-century BCE Persian report as the Indus country; reading a foreign source's name for India is LO-98.
Assertion-reason that outsiders named the land from the Indus because it was the first great landmark they met - the mechanism behind every foreign name, hence LO-98.
What 'India, that is Bharat' says about the country's identity - a question about the Constitution and the values it carries, so CG-SST3. No outcome under it covers naming the Union.
The Persian-held Indus country and its Sanskrit name Sindhu: the contact frame is LO-98 and the river itself is LO-82.
Sets Bharatavarsha as indigenous against India and Hind as foreign in origin; the contrast needs the outside names (LO-98) and the textual Indian one (LO-86).
Identifies the Vishnu Purana's 'snowy mountains' as the Himalayas - a textual definition (LO-86) resolved onto a physical feature (LO-82).
Finds the false name-to-language pairing (Indoi as Chinese) across Latin, Persian, Sanskrit and Greek; the discrimination is among the languages that named India from outside.
'Sindhava' in the Rig Vedic phrase traced to the Indus - the textual term (LO-86) resolved to the river (LO-82), matching the Sapta Sindhava items.
Persians as the intermediaries through whom Greek geographers first learned of India - a statement about the route of contact, so LO-98.
Bharat's Sanskrit roots against Hindustan's Persian ones; the comparison needs the indigenous textual name (LO-86) and the foreign coinage (LO-98).

Defines the subcontinent as a large peninsula projecting from Asia into the Indian Ocean - placement of a landmass against a continent and an ocean, which is LO-80. The item that merely asks the region's NAME was mapped to LO-81.
Names the Indian Subcontinent as the region covering India and its neighbours; LO-81 is the outcome that names neighbouring countries.
Names a natural boundary - the Himalayas, Hindu Kush or the seas. These are India's physical features, so LO-82 rather than the world-map outcome.
'Bharatavarsha' as the country of the Bharatas - the meaning of a name carried by the ancient texts, so LO-86.
Resolves the textual 'Cape Kumari' (LO-86) to today's Kanyakumari, India's southern tip (LO-82). Not LO-85, which is for historical sites rather than a physical cape.
Recall of the constitutional phrase itself; a Constitution item, so CG-SST3 with the other two.
The year the Constitution came into force, 1950. Constitutional fact, hence CG-SST3, not LO-90, since no historical development is being synthesised.
That Persian 'Hindu' named a place and not a religion - a correction about how outsiders used the word, so LO-98.
Indoi and Indike as the Greek names for India; a straight foreign-nomenclature recall.
Why Greek dropped the initial h from Hindu - a linguistic detail of the transmission from Persia to Greece, so LO-98.
Names a Chinese term for India (Yintu, Yindu or Tianzhu); the Chinese branch of the foreign-names set.
The language of the first 'Hindustan' inscription, Persian. The point is whose language coined it, which is LO-98, not LO-84's classification of inscriptions as sources.
The Latin name India - the step between Greek Indike and the modern English word, so LO-98.
The French 'Inde' continues the same chain of names taken up outside India; the only outcome covering how other lands named the country.
How the idea of India changed over millennia from fluid to fixed borders - a synthesis across periods, so LO-90 rather than a single geography outcome.
What Sapta Sindhava says about the north-west: a Rig Vedic name (LO-86) describing the Indus river system (LO-82).
The origin of Bharatavarsha in the Bharata people and its spread to the whole subcontinent - content from the Mahabharata and Vedic texts, so LO-86.
Ashoka's own reading of Jambudvipa, known from his inscriptions (LO-89), covering lands that are now neighbouring countries (LO-81).
Quotes the Vishnu Purana's definition of Bharata between ocean and snowy mountains: a textual formulation (LO-86) of India's physical limits (LO-82).
Why the Greeks said Indoi - taken from Persian and reshaped to their own sounds; a transmission question, so LO-98.
Links Chinese Yintu back to Sindhu through intermediate forms - the same foreign-transmission theme, in the Chinese case.
Xuanzang studying in India and carrying Buddhist manuscripts home to translate; an exchange in RELIGION and learning, which LO-98 names outright.
How Hindustan entered use, from a Persian inscription to later invaders' usage - a foreign name and its career, so LO-98.
Names the Indus, Ganga, Yamuna and Brahmaputra as the rivers that built the plains - India's physical features, squarely LO-82.
Describes the Himalayan and Hindu Kush northern boundary; a physical-feature item like the natural-boundary recall, and again LO-82.

Asks what ROLE ancient texts play as sources for the names - that is the use of literary sources in reconstruction (LO-84), illustrated from the texts' contents (LO-86). This is the one item in the chapter that is about sources as such.
How foreign travellers' and chroniclers' accounts supplied Hind, Indoi and Yintu: foreign literary sources used as evidence (LO-84) arising from contact outside India (LO-98).
